_authority: Every row below was DERIVED, not remembered, and the derivation is the interesting part. The audit asked one question no gate in this repo was asking: of the grammar's 152 named node types, which ones does the analyzer NEVER NAME? The set came from the analyzer's own source — its `case` labels (21 types it decides on) plus every type it compares or looks up (41 more) — leaving 100 that appear in neither list. Bucketing those 100 by inspection would have been a guess dressed as an inventory, so each candidate was PROBED instead, and probing found eight real defects that no existing gate could see, because in every one of them the COMMON spelling worked and only a rarer one was dark. The defects: `braced_variable` stored its braces, so `${a}` and `$a` became two symbols; `expandable_here_string_literal` was not in the switch at all, so a here-string published no read and, once forced, published it a line high with the line break and the sigil inside the target; the four `*_increment_expression`/`*_decrement_expression` types emitted nothing; a compound assignment published no read of its left side; a SPLAT (`@name`) kept its `@`; a variable passed as a command ARGUMENT was not read at all, which is the largest of them; a dynamic method target was published as `calls -> $method`; and an invocation-operator target could publish a line-break-bearing fragment. The instrument that found them is committed as the fixture: a line-level check over all 25,991 variable-reference edges in the corpora, asking whether the declared line actually contains the variable. It read 96.75% on the first run and 100.00% with zero residue after the fixes, and the last row of that residue is what exposed the dynamic method target. The corpora moved from 114,096 to 130,251 relationships across 760 files with symbols unchanged at 2,588/573 and unknownTargets/dupKeys/reservedTargets all still 0 — a pure read-addition, which is what a completeness gap should look like when it is closed.
_wave: M14 lane wave, powershell (issue #277 'Analyzer powershell: reach L5 SCOPED-VERIFIED'). This file is the F9 completeness section: it existed NOWHERE for this lane — powershell was one of 31 languages with a completeness spec and the only m14 lane without one — so 'is the analyzer complete over the language' had no answer beyond what the fixtures happened to touch.

handled_verified._description: Node types the analyzer consults at a type position AND whose behaviour is pinned by a committed fixture. The 21 `case` labels are decided on outright; the other 30 are the types it compares or looks up, each pinned by a fixture that would fail if the behaviour changed. Eleven of these were NOT handled when this inventory was written and are the direct result of the audit above: `braced_variable`, `expandable_here_string_literal`, the four counter-update types, `sub_expression`'s siblings, and the argument-read path. Three families of evidence: variable-reads-psa4 (spelling, splat, here-string, counter, compound, dynamic method), class-inherit-psa2 + method-scope-psb3 (classes, interfaces, inheritance), new-object-psa3 (construction), member-reads-psb5 (reads), data-shapes-psb10 (data), suppression-and-params-psb7 (parameters), payload-psb11 (payload and docstrings), per-site-lines-psb2 (per-site lines), reserved-words-psb4 (keyword suppression), module-surface-psb9 (module surface), file-owner-psa1 (ownership). `comment` is deliberately NOT in this bucket: the analyzer emits no relationship for a comment, it only READS the text for comment-based help, which PSD6 rules rather than this bucket asserting. A type in two buckets is a type the gate cannot check, so the classification follows what is emitted.

internal_silent._description: Structural containers, expression-ladder wrappers, literals and grammar plumbing that correctly emit nothing. This is the bucket where a lazy inventory would hide a real gap, so each family was checked rather than assumed. (1) THE EXPRESSION LADDER — `additive_expression`, `bitwise_expression`, `comparison_expression`, `format_expression`, `logical_expression`, `multiplicative_expression`, `range_expression` and their six `*_argument_expression` twins, plus the four operator leaves. These are a precedence chain, not constructs: PowerShell evaluates through them and emits nothing at any level, so a relationship at one would be the same fact recorded twice. CORRECTION (M60, measured): the sentence this bucket used to carry -- "a file of pure arithmetic publishes no edges and no symbols" -- was FALSE, and an adversarial probe is what caught it. Measured on a literals-only arithmetic file: 5 symbols and 4 `contains` edges, because every assignment declares a variable. What is true, and what this bucket actually claims, is narrower: the LADDER emits no edge of its own. A ladder that carried variable READS would be a different question, and it is a real asymmetry rather than a settled one -- `$acc += 2` publishes `uses -> acc` (compound-assignment reads are a deliberate fix) while `$p + $q` and `$m -lt $n` publish no read edge at all. So: the ladder is correctly silent, the OPERANDS' reads are unaddressed, and the two are different claims that had been written as one. Probe: script/m60/powershell-silent-bucket-probe.ts. (2) TYPE PLUMBING — `type_name`, `type_identifier`, `array_type_name`, `generic_type_name`, `generic_type_arguments`, `dimension`, `attribute_name`, `attribute_argument(s)`. The analyzer reads the TYPE OUT of these (PS24: a class-typed member is the only edge between two classes in one file) and publishes the type name; the wrapper itself declares nothing. (3) LITERALS — `decimal_integer_literal`, `hexadecimal_integer_literal`, `verbatim_string_characters`, `verbatim_here_string_characters`. A literal is a value, not a symbol; the 11 bare-number `uses` rows the oracle expected are this bucket. (4) SWITCH PLUMBING — `switch_body`, `switch_clauses`, `switch_clause_condition`, `switch_condition`, `switch_parameter(s)`, `switch_filename`. `switch_clause` itself is NOT here: it is handled, because a `switch` case is a decision point and counting it is what stops a ten-case switch measuring a cyclomatic complexity of 1 (PS13, measured at 174 uncounted nodes in the production draw). (5) CONTROL PLUMBING — `else_clause`, `elseif_clauses`, `finally_clause`, `catch_clauses`, `catch_type_list`, `for_condition`, `for_initializer`, `for_iterator`, `while_condition`, `label`, `label_expression`, `parenthesized_expression`, `array_expression`, `hash_literal_body`, `invokation_foreach_expression`, `path_command_name`, `path_command_name_token`, `foreach_parameter`, `named_block_list`, `program`. Each is a container whose CONTENTS are handled; the container is not itself a declaration. `program` is here deliberately: PS1 ruled that the FILE is the module and that no synthetic `global` scope symbol is ever emitted, so `program` must publish nothing.

gap._description: Confirmed unemitted semantics. An open gap is a tracked work item, never a gate failure — the gate fails when a gap exists that no design_decision rules, and when a ruling names a node type the wasm no longer produces. There are NO OPEN GAPS in this lane, and that is a measured statement rather than an omission: all eight defects the audit found are FIXED, each with a fixture row and a mutant, and the last of them (the dynamic method target) was the final non-justified row of the line-level check at 100.00%. The rows below are the CLOSED defects, recorded with their fix and their pin rather than deleted, because a completeness inventory that only ever says 'nothing is missing' is indistinguishable from one nobody wrote.

gaps.missing: `${a}` was stored as the symbol `{a}`, so the braced spelling and the plain spelling of one variable were two symbols and the read dangled. Measured: `$a = 1` declared `a`, a string containing `${a}` published `uses -> {a}`.
gaps.ruling: FIXED in `stripDollar`, which now collapses `${name}` to `name`, and in the read pass, which now enters on `braced_variable` as well as `variable`. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's `braced` rows and its `{braced}` forbidSymbol, plus the `braced-variable-keeps-braces` mutant.

gaps.missing: A here-string published no read at all while the identical text in a double-quoted string did, because this is a DIFFERENT node type from `expandable_string_literal` and only the latter was in the switch. Forcing a read then exposed two further faults: the grammar gives the interpolation a span starting at the end of the PREVIOUS line, so the edge was a line high, and its target carried the line break and the sigil — `uses -> "\n$message"`.
gaps.ruling: FIXED: the node type is in the switch, the read pass trims the text, and the line stamp skips the leading break. The grammar was NOT changed and should not be — the span is the text the interpolation occupies. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's two here-string rows, whose LINE NUMBERS are the assertion, plus the `here-string-interpolation-unread` mutant.

gaps.missing: `$n++` and `++$n` read their operand and published nothing, so all four types emitted no edge of any kind. A `uses` is the right edge: the write half has no edge in this lane's model, because a write to a local is not a fact the graph can express.
gaps.ruling: FIXED, and the fix had a HALF in it that the error count could not see: the operand is found by a bounded DESCENDANT search, because `++$n` nests it as `pre_increment_expression > unary_expression > variable` while `$n++` puts it directly under the node. A direct-child lookup found both postfix forms and silently missed both prefix forms — two of four sites missing, which reads as a partial success. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's four counter rows with their `isPostfix` metadata, the `counter-update-operand-unread` mutant, and the `prefix-counter-missed` mutant, which fails on its own if the prefix forms are the ones dropped.

gaps.missing: A COMPOUND assignment read its left side and published nothing: `$total += 1` is a read of `$total` and a write to it, the write was the declaration, and the read was nowhere. A plain `=` correctly publishes no read, so the OPERATOR is the entire distinction.
gaps.ruling: FIXED by reading the operator's own text, which is what keeps the plain assignment from gaining a read edge it does not have. The operand is found with the same `findDescendantVariable` helper the DECLARATION uses, so the read and the declaration cannot drift apart on a different depth constant — the left side sits at the bottom of an eleven-level expression ladder, and the neighbouring member-write search uses depth 14 for the same reason. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's two compound rows with their `assignmentOperator` metadata and the `compound-assignment-read-dropped` mutant.

gaps.missing: A variable passed as a command ARGUMENT was not read: `Write-Host $a` published the call edge and no `uses` at all, so every variable handed to a cmdlet was invisible while the same variable interpolated in a string was read. The largest of the eight — reading command arguments took the corpora from 114,096 to 130,251 relationships across 760 files.
gaps.ruling: FIXED, and it is the one fix that was WRONG on the first run. The pass read into `element_access` and published the RECEIVER, which PS9's ruling forbids by name — `member-reads-psb5` has a forbid row for exactly that pre-fix shape of form 4 — and the fixture failed on the run that introduced it. That is the gate working: +16,155 edges is not a licence to add a shape a fixture has already ruled on. The pass now skips script blocks (a block is a scope, and descending would attribute its locals to the caller) and skips `element_access` (PS9's target is the KEY, which the dedicated case already reads at the right grain). Pin: variable-reads-psa4's argument rows, the `variable-argument-not-read` mutant, and the `uses == 15` count, which is chosen so a receiver-reading regression scores 16.

gaps.missing: A SPLAT kept its `@`: the grammar models `@name` as a `variable` node whose text carries no sigil, so the dollar-strip did nothing and `New-PSOptions @OptionsArguments` published `uses -> @OptionsArguments` — a name no symbol can have.
gaps.ruling: FIXED in the read pass, stripping one leading `@` from a `variable` node's text. `@()` and `@{}` are array- and hashtable literals and arrive as `array_literal_expression` and `hash_literal_expression`, never as `variable`, so they cannot reach it. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's splat row and its `@splatArgs` forbidSymbol.

gaps.missing: A DYNAMIC method target was published as `calls -> $method`, which is wrong twice: a variable is stored stripped, so `$method` is a name no symbol can have, and the source says the method is CHOSEN AT RUNTIME, so calling a method named `$method` asserts a fact the code does not contain.
gaps.ruling: FIXED: a `$`-prefixed member is a VARIABLE holding a method name, so it is published as a `uses` of that variable with `isDynamicMethodTarget`. Found on ConstrainedLanguageRestriction.Tests.ps1:513 as the LAST row of the line-level check's residue, at which point the check read 100.00%. Pin: variable-reads-psa4's `isDynamicMethodTarget` row and its `calls -> $method` forbid row.

gaps.missing: An invocation-operator target could publish a line-break-bearing fragment as a `uses` name: on a line reading `$type::$method()` the command-name node held `$method()` plus the rest of the recovered line, so the stripped target was `method()\n                }`.
gaps.ruling: FIXED by guarding the invoked name with a plausibility predicate. The predicate exists because `unknownTargets` could not catch this: it asks whether a target MATCHES a symbol, and a target containing a newline matches nothing exactly as quietly as a correct one matches something, so these sat at 0 unknown for as long as they existed. Pin: the line-level check, which is the only instrument in the lane that sees this class.

design_decision.description: The powershell lane's contract. Each decision names the question, the answer, and what pins it. Where a decision removed a behaviour, the removed behaviour and its measurement are recorded — the four below are RULED-SILENT node types, meaning the analyzer deliberately publishes nothing for them, and each says why publishing something would be a fabrication rather than a fact. SPEC SHAPE 2026-10-17: PSD7-PSD10 are RELATIONSHIP-level rulings (externality metadata, overrides emission, ambiguous-target resolution, noDeclarationInFile) and carry NO `node_type` BY DESIGN — the inventory gate comma-splits that field into its classified-type set, and prose there would enter four meaningless tokens. See `_spec_shape_2026_10_17`.

decisions.question: `break`, `continue`, `return`, `throw` and `exit` are grammar `command` nodes, so does a keyword in command position become a call?
decisions.resolution: RULED: NO. PS5's reserved-word guard drops them before the call edge. A `calls` edge naming a language keyword can never resolve to a stored command, and this was measured rather than assumed — the pre-wave lane emitted keyword-named edges in the corpus, including the named blocks `begin`/`process`/`end`/`clean`/`dynamicparam`, which the GRAMMAR models as `command` nodes. Pinned by reserved-words-psb4's forbid rows and the PS5 mutant, which re-adds the keyword set and is caught.

decisions.question: DSC resource types (`File`, `Registry`, `Environment`, …) and `Configuration` names are bare words in a script. Do they become symbols?
decisions.resolution: RULED: a DSC RESOURCE INSTANCE is a real declaration and IS published (PS5c, entered on STRUCTURE — a command carrying a script-block argument inside a configuration — rather than on a list of resource names, because a guess-list had already been tried and matched nothing in the corpora). But the resource TYPE name and the data-command plumbing publish nothing: the type is a DSC built-in the engine resolves, not a project symbol, and naming it produced 3 fabricated edges in one fixture and 6 keyword-named edges in the corpus before the fix. Pinned by data-shapes-psb10 and the reserved-word set.

decisions.question: Workflow keywords are `command` nodes. Do they become calls?
decisions.resolution: RULED: NO. `parallel`, `sequence`, `workflow` and `inlinescript` are LANGUAGE KEYWORDS that the workflow subsystem resolves, in the same class as `class`/`enum`/`param` — they are in `LANGUAGE_KEYWORD_COMMANDS` and the guard drops them before the call edge. Pinned by reserved-words-psb4.

decisions.question: `--%` (stop-parsing) hands the rest of the line to a native command verbatim. Does the verbatim text become an argument?
decisions.resolution: RULED: NO. After `--%` PowerShell performs NO further parsing, so the text is not PowerShell at all — it is the native command's own argv. Publishing it as a PowerShell argument would attribute native syntax to a language that never saw it, and the grammar models the remainder as an opaque `verbatim_command_argument` for exactly this reason. The `stop_parsing` node itself is the marker the analyzer keys on to stop reading arguments.

decisions.question: Redirection carries a file name: `Get-Log > out.txt`. Does `out.txt` become a symbol or a `uses`?
decisions.resolution: RULED: NO for the OPERATORS and the redirection structure; the redirected file name is recorded as structure, not as a project symbol, because it names a file the script WRITES rather than one it depends on, and a `uses` edge would assert a dependency in the wrong direction. This ruling is also what made the G8/G9 `--flag=$var` residue safe to leave open: the `redirection` rule is the competing route that steals a glued value, and changing that is recorded as work rather than done quietly. Pinned by the F11 gate on every admitted grammar patch, which is where a redirection-stealing regression would surface first.

decisions.question: A comment is not code. Does it publish anything?
decisions.resolution: RULED: comments publish no SYMBOL and no relationship, and are the one place this lane reads raw TEXT — comment-based help (`.SYNOPSIS`) is the documentation source, and `extractRequiresModule` reads `#requires -Module` from a comment body, because comments are opaque to the grammar and no AST route exists. That is the sanctioned exception to the zero-regex policy and it is why `isSpaceCode` spells out all 25 code points JavaScript's `\s` matches rather than approximating: the comment delimiters are matched by character, not by a pattern. Pinned by payload-psb11's `expectDocstring`/`forbidDocstring` rows and the PS23 mutant.

decisions.question: `npx tsx script/m14/incoming-gate.ts powershell ps1 60` read `1192 ambiguous + 5877 unresolved of 9911 edges` with `markedExternal 0`, yet 1,938 of those 5,877 edges already carried this analyzer's own externality reading (`externalTarget` + `externalVia`, PS-B16). Why did the arbiter see none of them, and what may be marked?
decisions.resolution: RULED: THE CLAIM WAS PUBLISHED UNDER A KEY THE ARBITER DOES NOT READ. `incoming-gate.ts` takes a claim from the EXPLICIT list `EXTERNAL_KEYS` (script/m14/incoming-rule.ts) and `externalTarget` is not in it, so all 1,938 edges arrived unmarked — and an unmarked external is indistinguishable at the gate from a broken edge. PS38 adds `isExternalTarget: true` (in the list, same claim word for word) on exactly the edges the existing reading marks: the `declaredInFile(target)` guard and `externalReadingOf` are unchanged and NOT ONE EDGE IS ADDED. The second half of PS38 restricts WHERE it is published, because `verifyExternalClaim` asks about the TARGET ITSELF when there is no dotted owner (and refuses to ask at all for a non-identifier spelling) but asks about the OWNER — a string the edge does not name — when there is one: measured over the whole 978-file corpus, 82 marked edges were REFUTED and every one of the 82 had a BARE owner (`Text.UTF8Encoding` refuted by an unrelated declaration in Grace/scripts/capture-artifact-size.ps1:115; `powershell.exe`; `#requires -Version 3.0`'s owner `3`; `Test.User32::GetPlacement`, ConsoleHost.Tests.ps1:1075, whose owner `Test` is `class Test` in Scripting.Classes.BasicParsing.Tests.ps1:508), ZERO had a qualified owner. So the readable key is published only where the arbiter asks about the target itself or about an owner that is ITSELF QUALIFIED (`System.IO` in `System.IO.Path::Combine`); 49 edges at `powershell ps1 60` are withheld and keep the old key. MEASURED AFTER: `powershell ps1 60` — FAIL, 1192 ambiguous + **3988 unresolved** of 9911, with 1889 marked external = 178 verified + 1711 unverifiable + **0 REFUTED**; the whole-corpus arm (`--nf 60 --all`, 978 files, 160,306 edges) reads unresolved **75,964 -> 50,558**, 2,296 verified, 23,110 unverifiable, **0 refuted**, at a payload cost of +642,552 B (1.815% of the lane's relationship JSON). BEFORE/AFTER are both in validation/m14/fixtures/powershell/measurements/ (incoming-gate-ps1-60-{before,after-narrowed}.json, incoming-split-ps1-60-all-{before,after-narrowed}.json), and the census re-measures the gate's own numbers exactly (`COMPARE ... AGREE`). Pinned by fixture powershell/externality-arbiter-psb17 (19 fixture files pass): every positive row has a negative twin of the same spelling shape, including the withheld broad-owner row. NOT DONE, and measured as such: the obvious widening (mark every command-position `noDeclarationInFile` call) is PSD10.

decisions.question: `overrides` is SILENT in the firing instrument (`bun script/m14/firing-check.mjs POWERSHELL`, 120-file stride). Does the language have the construct at all, and if so does the type EMIT it or is the emission missing? A silent type in a stride sample is not evidence about the type.
decisions.resolution: RULED: THE CONSTRUCT EXISTS AND `overrides` EMITS — the SILENCE IS A SAMPLING ARTIFACT, measured on the WHOLE corpus in two instruments. (1) `npx tsx validation/m14/fixtures/powershell/pass3-probes.ts --only P15` over all 1,181 admitted files (tree census, 0 shard failures): **273 class declarations** (chain-depth histogram 0:247, 1:22, 2:4), **26 classes carry a base-type clause declared in the SAME file**, **12 hop-1 derived/base member pairs** exist under the analyzer's own first-match-wins rule, and **12 of 12 are published** (`hop1PairsTheAnalyzerPublishes: 12`, `transitivePairsItMisses: 0`). (2) The firing instrument at its own default (120 of the corpus, even stride) reads `8 types fired — implements overrides SILENT`; at `NFILES=1000 bun script/m14/firing-check.mjs POWERSHELL` — the whole admitted population, no sampling cut — it reads `10 types fired ... overrides:12 implements:3`: every one of the ten relationship types fires and NOTHING is silent. The artifacts are committed: validation/m14/fixtures/powershell/measurements/overrides-p15-corpus.json. WHY THE STRIDE MISSED IT: all 12 published `overrides` edges come from ONE file, `powershell/test/powershell/Language/Classes/scripting.Classes.inheritance.tests.ps1` (extends=33 there; 13 corpus files carry a base clause at all), so a 120-file stride over 400 admits it with probability ~30% and the 400-file stride happened to skip it too (`NFILES=400` reads 9 types fired, overrides still silent — implements fires there). UNEXERCISED AND NAMED AS SUCH: the hop-2+ branch of the chain walk (0 transitive pairs in the corpus) and the derived-property-over-base-property case (0 sites); P15 reports both rather than calling the matcher correct. No analyzer change was needed and none was made for this type.

decisions.question: After the externality re-spelling, `incoming-gate.ts powershell ps1 60` reads 1,192 AMBIGUOUS of 9,911 edges — 30% of the sample and now the lane's dominant number. Is any of it reducible without changing edge identity?
decisions.resolution: RULED: IRREDUCIBLE AT 1,192, and the split is the evidence, not the number. `npx tsx validation/m14/fixtures/powershell/incoming-split.mts --nf 60 --all` (the gate's rule imported, 978 files parsed, 219 distinct names behind the 1,192 edges) splits the column by WHY the declarations collide: **multiFile 927 (77.8%)** — the colliding declarations are in DIFFERENT files of the same repository; PowerShell binds a bare name at RUN TIME against session state (dot-source, the caller's scope chain, module exports), so no field an edge can carry names which file's declaration is meant, and the language has no spelling for it at the reference site (`$expected` is declared in 6 files of one repo, 9 declarations, and every Pester `It` block has its own); **oneFileDiffOwner 142** — one file, different owner scopes; **oneFileSameOwnerDiffKind 123** — one file, one owner, and the name is published under two KINDS (kind signatures over the colliding declarations: variable 546, property|variable 323, property 297, class|property 22, constructor 4 — a variable and a hashtable key of one spelling, or a property and its backing field, are DIFFERENT symbols and the store must keep both); **oneFileSameOwnerSameKind 0**. Nothing in the column is an analyzer defect: every colliding name is a name the analyzer was asked to publish, and the only sub-class with a conceivable repair (the 123 kind-distinct groups, 10.3%) would need the analyzer to stop publishing one of two distinct symbols, which changes SYMBOL identity to move a resolution metric. Corpus-wide the same walk reads 48,866 ambiguous of 160,306 edges (30.5%), so the sample is not an outlier. Recorded rather than chased, per the ROUND brief: a column that cannot move without deleting facts is ruled with counts.

decisions.question: The re-spelling leaves 3,988 unresolved at `powershell ps1 60`. A candidate widening would mark the 2,104 command-position `calls` edges carrying `noDeclarationInFile` — bare command names the emitting file declares nowhere — which the census measures as 2,099 that would VERIFY, 5 that would be unverifiable and 0 refuted. Why is it not shipped?
decisions.resolution: RULED: REJECTED, because the fact it rests on is not an externality claim. `noDeclarationInFile` was introduced by this lane as a FACT about the emitting file ('this file declares no symbol with that spelling') and its own docstring rules it non-actionable: 'a `$local` no file declares and a cmdlet are indistinguishable under it, and only the second is external by construction'. The widening's class has no shape evidence at all — measured members are `dotnet`, `WriteLine`, `Describe`, `Context`, `It`, `Should` — so a typo'd or undefined function name would be published as external with nothing behind it but the absence of a declaration, which is exactly the shape the ROUND brief warns about (a lane marked 435 edges on a plausible rule, audited them, and found 82 naming functions the same repository declares; it withdrew the change). THE AUDIT THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT HERE, run before shipping: of the 2,102-edge class, **74 name a declaration the SAME repository publishes** (whole-corpus declaration truth), 3.5% — they resolve at production scope, where the mark would ride along on a resolved edge and never be checked. The gain is real and is recorded rather than hidden: unresolved 3,988 -> ~1,884 at sample scope. It is declined because this lane's externality rule requires a SPELLING reading plus the declaration guard (`externalReadingOf`), and breaking that rule to move a column is the fabrication the rule exists to prevent.

decisions.question: A dot-sourced path is a PROJECT FILE reference, not an external target — but WHICH paths? The first incident's rule answered 'a relative path ending in .ps1', and the ARBITER asks a different question: 'is this path one of the PROJECT's admitted files?' (pathTargetInProject, script/m14/incoming-rule.ts). The two disagree on three axes: the EXTENSION (the gate admits `powershell: "ps1,psm1,psd1"` — incoming-gate.ts:134 — and the arbiter's match is by SUFFIX, so the extension is irrelevant to it and decisive to the rule), the SEPARATOR (the arbiter matches a BARE `Helper.psm1` against any admitted file with that basename, so a separator requirement hides nothing), and the ABSOLUTE case (the gate's project facts are REPO-RELATIVE — path.relative(repoRoot, abs), incoming-gate.ts:577 — so an absolute path can never be refuted, and withholding it discards a TRUE claim). Which spelling may carry an externality reading?
decisions.resolution: RULED: A RELATIVE path naming one of the lane's ADMITTED spellings carries NO externality reading, and a path that names something OUTSIDE any project KEEPS it. The 2026-10-19 rule (a relative path ending in .ps1) was correct for the two rows it was written for and too narrow in two directions, and BOTH were measured. (1) THE SECOND REFUTED CLAIM: powershell/test/powershell/Modules/Microsoft.PowerShell.Security/FileCatalog.Tests.ps1:365 and :366 publish `uses -> DSCResources\UserConfigProviderModVersion1\UserConfigProviderModVersion1.psm1` with `externalTarget: true`, and that file IS in the project — the arbiter's own `verifyExternalClaim` answers `externalRefuted` on both. The lane's extFAIL column read 0 anyway, because PS38 withholds the arbiter-readable key on a bare owner and `externalTarget` is not in EXTERNAL_KEYS, so the false claim was published AND INVISIBLE. The 2026-10-19 rule missed it because .psm1 is not .ps1. MEASURED, whole population (1,181 files / 30 repos, root $HOME/fixtures/repositories and the .corpus symlink farm, which admit the SAME multiset of (repo, relative path)): 47 distinct target spellings name an admitted project file — 26 .ps1, 13 .psm1, 8 .psd1 — and 2 of them were published as claims. (2) THE DISCARDED TRUE CLAIM: /usr/lib/x.ps1 and C:\x.ps1 were WITHHELD by the 2026-10-19 rule (it matched any .ps1 carrying a separator), and the arbiter could have checked them. The rule now withholds the reading when the target ends in .ps1, .psm1 or .psd1 AND its spelling is a RELATIVE path — not /unix-rooted, not C:\drive, not a URI scheme — which is the bash lane's rule applied to powershell's own admitted spellings. _spec_shape_2026_10_17.why: FOUR `design_decision` RECORDS CARRIED PROSE IN `node_type`. The inventory gate COMMA-SPLITS that field into its classified-type set, so `"relationship metadata: externalTarget/externalVia (…) -> isExternalTarget"` entered it as four meaningless tokens. The same defect shape the fleet found in lua's `gaps[].node_type` (sentences split into nothing, 46 of 48 types left in no bucket) — here it was harmless ONLY because all 154 wasm types are already covered by handled/silent/PSD1-6, so the garbage could not mask an unclassified type. Fixed rather than left because 'harmless today' is how a spec rots.
_spec_shape_2026_10_17.rule: A record whose `node_type` names no grammar node type must not carry the field at all — the gate's own loadSpec skips node_type-less decisions (`if (!d.node_type) continue`) precisely so a relationship-level ruling classifies nothing.
